# The Best Alternatives to Magnifi in 2026


COMPARISON


Magnifi alternatives


Magnifi, VideoVerse's AI clipping product, did something genuinely useful: it convinced a lot of rights holders that a machine could find the moments in a game and cut them without an editor scrubbing a timeline. Plenty of teams, leagues and broadcasters started there.


What most of them discover a season in is that finding moments was never the whole job. The job is a finished, on-brand, correctly framed package sitting in the social team's hands while the game is still being talked about. That is where evaluations start again, and it is why we get so many calls that open with "we already have clipping."


Below is a straight read on the alternatives worth putting on your shortlist in 2026.


## 1. Narrative Sports, the best Magnifi alternative


We build the layer that takes a live feed or an archive file and returns finished media and structured data at the same time. Every event, player and team is tagged frame-accurately as the game runs, each moment carries a virality score, and the clips come back cut to 9:16, 1:1 and 16:9 with the action reframed rather than centre-cropped. First clips land in well under a minute of the moment happening.


The three things that decide most switches away from a clipping-only tool:


**Clips and data from one pass.** The same model that cuts the highlight writes the event record behind it, so you get a queryable per-player data set out of footage that previously carried no data at all. You are not paying one vendor to watch the game and a second one to describe it.


**Packages, not just clips.** Individual moments are the easy half. Narrative assembles full recaps and packages to an exact runtime, in order, with walk-on and final whistle toggled on or off, and hands you a browser editor with real multi-track editing when you want the last ten percent by hand.


**A real API.** Full REST access, event webhooks and scoped keys, so clipping becomes a step inside your own pipeline rather than a portal somebody has to remember to log into. Teams that have outgrown a UI-first tool tend to feel this one immediately.


**The best output at the lowest price.** Broadcast-grade cuts, clean reframing and tagging accurate enough to build a data set on, priced for the operation you actually run rather than the one an enterprise deck assumes. No seven-figure minimums, no per-clip surprises, and no quality trade to get there. Teams comparing us against both the incumbents and the cheap tools usually find we are the only quote that beats them on both axes at once.


It also travels across sports. The same system runs football, soccer, basketball, hockey, tennis and squash, which matters if you are an athletic department or a federation with more than one property to service.


## 2. WSC Sports


The enterprise incumbent, and the most direct comparison if your operation is a major league or a national broadcaster. Deep integrations, a long track record, and pricing and onboarding scoped accordingly. Strong if you fit the profile it was built for; heavy if you are a single club, a college department or a growing league.


## 3. Grabyo


Cloud production and distribution first, clipping second. Good at getting a cut out to a lot of destinations quickly and at letting a distributed team work in a browser. Less of an answer if what you want is the machine deciding what is worth cutting in the first place.


## 4. Pixellot and Spiideo


Capture-led platforms. If you do not have a broadcast feed at all, an automated camera system plus its own highlight layer solves the acquisition problem and the content problem together. The trade is that you are buying into their capture stack, and the output is tuned to what that camera saw.


## 5. Greenfly


Not a clipper. It is where clips go: collection, rights-managed distribution, and getting assets into the hands of athletes, sponsors and partners. Frequently the thing sitting downstream of whatever you choose above, rather than a replacement for it.


## How to run the evaluation


Give every vendor the same game file, ideally an awkward one: bad lighting, an unusual camera angle, a sport that is not the one in their demo reel. Then measure four things. How long until the first publishable clip. How many clips a human had to touch. Whether the vertical cut actually follows the play. And whether you got any data back you could query afterward, or just video files.


Most teams find the first three are close between the serious options and the fourth is where the field thins out fast.
